## Project Overview

This report details a time series forecasting project designed to
predict daily cyclist volumes on Johnston St. Bridge in Victoria, BC.
The pipeline executes data preparation, model training, validation
backtesting, and out-of-sample forecasting for 30 days in November 2025.

### Victoria's Critical Active Transportation Artery

-   The **Johnson Street Bridge** serves as a vital multi-use link
    connecting downtown Victoria with regional trail networks.
-   **Objective:** Build an end-to-end predictive pipeline to forecast
    daily cyclist volumes.
-   **Business Value:** Empower infrastructure management to optimize
    seasonal maintenance windows and accurately evaluate environmental
    transit ROI.

## Preliminaries

### Data

As shown below, the time series shows high-frequenzy daily cyclist volumes over
approximately 5 years. The series exhibits strong seasonality, with the primary
variation appearing in days, and appears to be generally increasing over time. 
An interesting observation of this data is that the minimum number of cyclists appear to remain constant across time, while the maximum number of cyclists increases over time.




```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5

library(ggplot2)
library(scales)

# Get the start date of the data
start_date <- min(bikes$date, na.rm = TRUE)

# Build explicit yearly breaks starting from that date
custom_breaks <- c(start_date, as.Date(c("2021-01-01", "2022-01-01", "2023-01-01", "2024-01-01", "2025-01-01", "2026-01-01")))

ggplot(bikes, aes(x = date, y = cyclists)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", size = 0.6) +
  scale_x_date(
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05)),
    breaks = custom_breaks,               
    labels = date_format("%Y")            
  ) + 
  labs(
    title = "Daily Cyclist Volume",
    subtitle = "Historical Baseline Observations: May 2020 - October 2025",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Number of Cyclists"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

```

In addition, unit root testing (using both Augmented Dickey Fuller (ADF)
and Kwiatkowski-Phillips-Schmidt-Shin (KPSS) tests) suggests that the number of cyclists is a
unit root process as we fail to reject the null of non-stationarity in the ADF test but
reject the null of stationarity in the KPSS test.

```{r}
#| label: formatted-stationarity-table
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(tseries)
library(dplyr)
library(gt)

# Execute the underlying diagnostic tests
adf_res  <- adf.test(bikes_ts, alternative = "stationary")

kpss_res <- kpss.test(bikes_ts, null = "Trend")

# Structure the results into a clean dataframe
stationarity_df <- data.frame(
  Test_Name = c("Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF)", "Kwiatkowski-Phillips-Schmidt-Shin (KPSS)"),
  Null_Hypothesis = c("Series possesses a unit root (Non-Stationary)", "Series is stationary around a trend (Stationary)"),
  Statistic = c(adf_res$statistic, kpss_res$statistic),
  P_Value = c(adf_res$p.value, kpss_res$p.value)
)

# Render a professional HTML table
stationarity_df %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Stationarity Tests for Daily Cyclist Volume",
    subtitle = "Joint Diagnostics for Unit Roots and Trend Stationary Dynamics"
  ) %>%
  cols_label(
    Test_Name = "Diagnostic Test",
    Null_Hypothesis = "Null Hypothesis (H₀)",
    Statistic = "Test Statistic",
    P_Value = "p-value"
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = Statistic,
    decimals = 4
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = P_Value,
    decimals = 4
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
    locations = cells_column_labels()
  ) %>%
  tab_options(
    table.width = pct(100),
    column_labels.background.color = "#f8f9fa",
    heading.title.font.size = px(18)
  )

``` 


The ACF plot shows slow decay in
the residuals, with spikes every seven days (each week), which indicates weekly dependence.
The PACF plot shows that the first lag is the most important, and suggests that
including at least 14 lags is important, as the 14th lag still has significance.



```{r}
#| label: raw-data-diagnostics
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(forecast)

# Configure the graphic window to display two plots side-by-side in one row
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

# Generate individual ACF and PACF plots without the automated middle time series panel
Acf(bikes_ts, main = "Raw Cyclist Volume ACF", lag.max = 35)
Pacf(bikes_ts, main = "Raw Cyclist Volume PACF", lag.max = 35)

# Reset the graphic layout parameters back to default
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

```

These plots suggest a highly persistent series, as the first lag on the PACF has a value of 0.89 and slow decay over time in the ACF plot with spikes every week.


### Variables

Exogenous weather variables are collected, including Mean Temperature (°C), 
Precipitation (mm), and Wind Speed (km/h). I also include indicators for 
days and months. I chose March as the baseline month
since roughly half of the months were higher or below, and the same for
Friday. 

Unlike heavy rail or closed motor vehicles, cyclists are
directly exposed to the surrounding climate. This exposure introduces
high-dimensional volatility; microclimatic shifts in rainfall duration,
ambient temperature bounds, wind speeds, and even daylight changes may
create massive fluctuations in cyclist demand. Furthermore, research
demonstrates that even incorrect public weather forecasts or heavy cloud
visuals actively alter a cyclist's morning modal choice before they
leave the house. Therefore, we will include weather data, which will be
forecasted weather data, and other exogenous controls to capture these
environmental and temporal effects.


## Model Selection


### ARIMA

Given the results from the preliminary analysis, a seasonal ARIMA
model with exogenous regressors is chosen to create the forecasts,. We account for the change in daily cyclists depending on the previous 14 days of changes,
ensuring stationarity by differencing our data once, and capturing one day shocks with MA(1).
For the seasonal component, AR(1) and MA(1) at lag 7 captures that the number of cyclists
today is highly related to the same weekday in the previous week in both value and error. This
captures the persistence and weekly patterns that are evidenced in our data. In choosing this
model, AIC and manual tinkering with model parameters (including several different lag
lengths) are used to pick the model with a realistic fit. Exactly what lag length to 
include is a bit of an art form, but the AIC is a good starting point.

Forecasting cyclist counts requires a statistical framework that can handle both historical momentum and external disruptions. The ARIMAX model, which stands for AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average with Exogenous Inputs, is an extension of standard time series modeling.

The autoregressive part captures the internal momentum, meaning that the number of riders on a trail today is often heavily related to how many people were riding yesterday. The integrated component applies differencing to stabilize the data, attempting to solve the serial correlation, stripping out long-term trends or seasonal shifts so the statistical properties remain constant over time. The moving average section corrects for sudden, short-term shocks to the system, like a minor traffic delay or a one-off event, by analyzing past forecast errors. Finally, the exogenous inputs act as the external anchors, allowing the model to incorporate outside datasets directly into the mathematical equation.

The foundational step involves checking for stationarity, typically via an Augmented Dickey-Fuller test, to ensure the data does not exhibit a continuous upward or downward drift that could bias our coefficients.

Once the model is fitted, the focus shifts entirely to the residuals, which are the differences between the predicted counts and the actual observed numbers. These residuals should behave as white noise, meaning they are completely random, unbiased, and contain no lingering information.

Now, the diagnostic testing for the ARIMAX model.


```{r}
#| label: arimax-diagnostics
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(forecast)

# Generate a unified layout displaying residual trends alongside ACF and PACF plots
ggtsdisplay(
  residuals(fit_arimax), 
  main = "ARIMAX Residual Diagnostic Architecture",
  theme = theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
)

```


```{r}
#| label: residual-normality-curve
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(ggplot2)

# Extract residuals and convert to a clean data frame
res_data <- data.frame(Residuals = as.numeric(residuals(fit_arimax)))

# Calculate baseline metrics for the normal curve overlay
res_mean <- mean(res_data$Residuals, na.rm = TRUE)
res_sd   <- sd(res_data$Residuals, na.rm = TRUE)

ggplot(res_data, aes(x = Residuals)) +
  # Plot empirical density histogram
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 40, fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7, color = "white") +
  # Overlay the theoretical normal bell curve
  stat_function(
    fun = dnorm, 
    args = list(mean = res_mean, sd = res_sd), 
    color = "darkred", 
    size = 1.2
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "ARIMAX Residual Distribution",
    subtitle = "Empirical Density vs. Theoretical Normal Curve",
    x = "Model Residuals (Error Magnitude)",
    y = "Density",
    caption = "Blue Bars = Empirical Residuals | Red Curve = Fitted Normal Distribution"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )

```


Evaluating the residual diagnostic architecture provides a transparent look into the health and mathematical validity of the fitted ARIMAX model before generating out-of-sample forecasts. The primary objective of this diagnostic phase is to verify that the model has successfully extracted all predictable systemic information from the historical dataset, leaving behind errors that behave purely as white noise.

From these tests, all looks to be quite well.The baseline timeline plot of the residuals reveals a highly stable, mean-reverting process that fluctuates uniformly around a mean of zero. The lack of widening or narrowing bands across the timeline indicates that the error variance remains constant over time. This absence of heteroskedasticity ensures that the model is not prone to volatile, compounding errors during specific historical periods, establishing a stable foundation for the forward-looking projection window.

Inspection of the ACF and PACF plots demonstrates the correlation coefficients across almost all immediate lags are successfully suppressed within the dashed statistical significance thresholds. 

However, minor visual anomalies emerge as isolated, marginal spikes breaching the blue significance boundaries at lag fourteen and lag twenty-eight. These boundaries indicate a tiny fraction of lingering bi-weekly and monthly seasonality that the linear lag structures did not perfectly absorb. In urban transit networks, such minor residual dependencies are common, often reflecting subtle real-world disruptions like bi-weekly employment pay cycles, statutory holiday shifts, or multi-week weather anomalies that slightly alter routine commuter behavioral patterns. Given that the surrounding lags remain completely quiet, these isolated breaches are minor enough to tolerate without risking structural model instability.

Finally, the residual distribution plot provides strong statistical confirmation regarding the required assumption of normality. The empirical density bars track the path of the fitted theoretical normal bell curve with exceptional symmetry, centering perfectly over the zero-error axis. The distribution exhibits no severe skewness and lacks heavy, outlying tails on either side. This clean normal profile gives evidence that the model's parameters are unbiased, confirming that the calculated prediction intervals for the final cyclist count forecasts are mathematically reliable and valid for infrastructure planning.



###  OLS

The value of forecasting does not have to just derive from prediction
accuracy. Forecasting does not have to be independent of an attempt of
causal inference, and some cases gives opportunity to be an extension of
the modelling process. In the case of forecasting cyclist traffic, our
goal is not just to give an accurate prediction of the number of
cyclists on a specific day, but to understand the underlying mechanisms
that are driving cyclist traffic.

This allows for the creation of policies that adapt to the underlying
mechanisms that may shift in response to an exogenous shock, such as
expanded bike infrastructure. This will help bridge the common pitfall
of structural breaks rendering an accurate model nearly useless.If we
can understand the underlying mechanisms that drive cyclist demand, we
can better adapt to these structural breaks and create more robust
forecasts.

To address this, we will use Linear Regression (OLS) as it is highly
interpretable.

One issue with OLS for causal inference in time series is, the
assumption that the error on any given day ($\epsilon_t$) tells you
nothing about the error on the next day. This is highly unlikely in time
series and this violation is serial correlation, or that other days will
impact today. This will deflate the standard errors, making our
coefficients seem more statistically significant than they are.

With this in mind, it is not a large issue for forecasting and we won't
make any causal claims.

To begin, I estimate an OLS model with the exogenous weather variables and
indicators for days and months. 

A few interesting patterns emerge. Firstly, it seems that the weather
coeffieints are consistent with theory. Ridership increases with
temperature (though here it is linear though likely is quadratic), and
decreases with precipitation and wind. This is consistent across our
months, as spring and summer months have higher ridership than that of
those in the winter months.

If you look at just the day section, it looks like this route is
primarily used by commuters, as the weekends are lower than Friday but most 
weekdays are associated with higher cyclist counts, on average. This is an important observation in itself, as it suggests targeting commuter ridership uses this infrastructure more than
recreational riders.

```{r}
#| label: categorized-ols-table-with-fit
#| echo: false

library(broom)
library(dplyr)
library(gt)

# 1. Pull the coefficients out cleanly
raw_estimates <- broom::tidy(fit_lm)

# 2. Assign interactive row groupings and display names
interactive_df <- raw_estimates %>%
  select(term, estimate) %>%
  mutate(
    Display_Name = case_when(
      term == "(Intercept)"                ~ "Baseline Intercept",
      term == "mean_temp"                  ~ "Mean Temperature (°C)",
      term == "precip_mm"                  ~ "Precipitation (mm)",
      term == "wind_mean_kmh"              ~ "Wind Speed (km/h)",
      
      term == "factor(month)01"            ~ "January",
      term == "factor(month)02"            ~ "February",
      term == "factor(month)03"            ~ "March",
      term == "factor(month)04"            ~ "April",
      term == "factor(month)05"            ~ "May",
      term == "factor(month)06"            ~ "June",
      term == "factor(month)07"            ~ "July",
      term == "factor(month)08"            ~ "August",
      term == "factor(month)09"            ~ "September",
      term == "factor(month)10"            ~ "October",
      term == "factor(month)11"            ~ "November",
      term == "factor(month)12"            ~ "December",
      
      term == "factor(day)Monday"          ~ "Monday",
      term == "factor(day)Tuesday"         ~ "Tuesday",
      term == "factor(day)Wednesday"       ~ "Wednesday",
      term == "factor(day)Thursday"        ~ "Thursday",
      term == "factor(day)Friday"          ~ "Friday",
      term == "factor(day)Saturday"        ~ "Saturday",
      term == "factor(day)Sunday"          ~ "Sunday",
      TRUE                                 ~ term
    ),
    Coefficient_Group = case_when(
      term %in% c("(Intercept)", "mean_temp", "precip_mm", "wind_mean_kmh") ~ "Meteorological Drivers",
      grepl("month", term)                                                  ~ "Monthly Seasonal Adjustments (March Baseline)",
      grepl("day", term)                                                    ~ "Daily Seasonal Adjustments (Friday Baseline)",
      TRUE                                                                  ~ "Model Settings"
    )
  ) %>%
  select(Coefficient_Group, Display_Name, estimate)

# 3. Pull overall model fit diagnostics using broom::glance()
fit_stats <- broom::glance(fit_lm)

# 4. Build the interactive HTML table
interactive_df %>%
  group_by(Coefficient_Group) %>%
  gt(rowname_col = "Display_Name") %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "OLS Baseline Parameter Architecture",
    subtitle = "Expanded Elasticities & Model Diagnostics"
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = estimate,
    decimals = 2
  ) %>%
  # Append the Model Fit Summary Statistics at the bottom
  tab_source_note(
    source_note = html(paste0(
      "<strong>Model Fit Diagnostics:</strong><br>",
      "Observations: ", format(fit_stats$nobs, big.mark = ","), " | ",
      "R²: ", round(fit_stats$r.squared, 3), " | ",
      "Adj. R²: ", round(fit_stats$adj.r.squared, 3), " | ",
      "RMSE: ", round(sqrt(mean(fit_lm$residuals^2)), 2), " | ",
      "AIC: ", format(round(fit_stats$AIC, 1), big.mark = ","), " | ",
      "BIC: ", format(round(fit_stats$BIC, 1), big.mark = ",")
    ))
  ) %>%
  opt_interactive(
    active = TRUE,
    use_search = TRUE
  ) %>%
  tab_options(
    table.width = pct(100),
    source_notes.background.color = "#f8f9fa" # Clean background block
  )
```

### XGBoost

The Extreme Gradient Boosting framework approaches urban transit forecasting by building a sequential chain of shallow decision trees that iteratively correct past errors. This strategy makes it exceptionally well-suited for capturing sharp, non-linear thresholds in human behavior—such as the exact rainfall volume that causes commuting habits to shift—without requiring manual interaction terms.

By mapping high-dimensional interactions between temporal schedules and meteorological conditions, the model automatically recognizes that an increase in ambient temperature alters cyclist counts differently on a weekend morning than it does during a midweek commuter rush. It creates localized boundaries that adapt to volatile microclimatic shifts without suffering from the rigid assumptions of global parameters.


## Backtesting

In time series forecasting, we can’t rely on a standard train-test split
where you randomly shuffle your data. Because time has a strict
direction, shuffling would let your model "peek into the future" to
predict the past, known as data leakage.

That is where backtesting comes in. It is the process of testing a
forecasting model's predictive accuracy by simulating how it would have
performed historically using actual past data.

It is a critical step in time series analysis, as it allows us to
evaluate the model's performance on unseen data and ensure that it
generalizes well to future observations. While a model that backtests
well is not guaranteed to perform well in the future, it is a strong
indicator of its potential effectiveness.

Additionally, it helps prevent overfitting, as we can assess how well
the model captures underlying patterns without being overly influenced
by noise in the training data.

### Evaluating Forecasts

How did the models preform? This is answered with a battery of metrics.
We should not put too much stake in any single metric, but take into
account all of our metrics.

If we consider the task of forecasting as if we were medical doctors,
metrics are just symptoms of the model's health (performance), and we
need to factor several symptoms (metrics) together to get a holistic
diagnosis of the model's health (performance). We combine these
evaluation metrics with our diagnostic testing for model assumptions to
get a complete picture of model health.

The metrics we will use are:

Mean Absolute Error (MAE) measures the average magnitude of the errors
in a set of forecasts, without considering their direction. It is the
average of the absolute differences between the actual values ($y_t$)
and predicted values ($\hat{y}_t$). The formula for MAE is:

$$MAE = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{t=1}^{n} |y_t - \hat{y}_t|$$

This treats all erros linearly, meaning that an error of say 50 cyclists
is considered twice as bad as an error of 25 cyclists.

One benefit is that we are using the exact units as the original data,
which makes it easy to interpret. However, it does not penalize larger
errors more than smaller ones. So, if our model is way off when there is
lots of rain, we don't penalize that specifically.

Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) squares the errors before averaging them,
and then takes the square root of the final result.

$$RMSE = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n} \sum_{t=1}^{n} (y_t - \hat{y}_t)^2}$$ The
Intuition: Because the errors are squared before they are averaged, RMSE
puts a much heavier penalty on large errors. An error of 10 results in a
penalty of 100, while an error of 5 is only 25.

Like MAE, it expresses the error in the original data units. However, it
heavily penalize large, systemic misses or unexpected spikes. If our MAE
is better than our RMSE, it indicates that we have a few large misses
that are dragging down our RMSE.

A single massive outlier during an unusual event (like a holiday or a
sudden data anomaly) can skew the RMSE upward, making a generally
excellent model look terrible.

Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) solves the scale problem by
expressing the error as a percentage of the actual values. Rather than
looking at nominal values, it looks at relative values. It is the
average of the absolute percentage differences between the actual values
($y_t$) and predicted values ($\hat{y}_t$).

$$MAPE = \frac{100\%}{n} \sum_{t=1}^{n} \left| \frac{y_t - \hat{y}_t}{y_t} \right|$$
This gives an idea about how far off we are, on average. Being off by 10
units when the actual value is 100 (10% error) is treated the same as
being off by 100 units when the actual value is 1,000.

This is a very intuitive metric, since being off by 10% on average gives
a better clue than 10 units. It also lets you compare model performance
across entirely different time series with different scales.

The division by $y_t$ is scary, since if our observations are close to
0, we can get a huge error. We also need to make sure that $y_t$ is
never 0, since we can't divide by 0. In our case, we are safe, since we
have no days with 0 cyclists.

### How did the models perform?

The out-of-sample evaluation metrics for the three models are summarized
in the table below. The metrics are calculated based on the forecasts
made for November 2025, comparing the predicted cyclist volumes against
the actual observed values.

```{r}

#| echo: false
#| include: false

library(gt)
library(dplyr)

# Convert the matrix into a clean dataframe for table formatting[cite: 5]
metrics_df <- as.data.frame(final_metrics) %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column(var = "Model Architecture")

# Create a professional HTML table
metrics_df %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "November 2025 Production Evaluation Results",
    subtitle = "Johnson Street Bridge Daily Cyclist Volume Forecasts"
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(MAE, RMSE),
    decimals = 2
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = MAPE,
    decimals = 2,
    pattern = "{x}%"
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
    locations = cells_column_labels()
  ) %>%
  tab_options(
    table.width = pct(100),
    column_labels.background.color = "#f8f9fa", # 🔥 Fixed the argument name here
    heading.title.font.size = px(18)
  )
```

Across all three metrics, XGBoost outperformed both the OLS and ARIMAX
models. The RMSE of 285.63 is quite close to its MAE of 233.18,
suggesting that isn't prone to extreme misses. With an MAPE of just
under 15%, it indicates that the model's predictions are, on average,
within 15% of the actual observed cyclist volumes. Considering the
forecasting window of 30 days, this should be considered quite accurate.

The ARIMAX model, while performing better than OLS, still lagged behind
XGBoost, indicating that the inclusion of exogenous variables alone was
not sufficient to achieve optimal forecasting accuracy.

One important note with this sort of open forecasting, where we depend
on a forecast for one or more of our independent variables such as
weather, it that the accuraccy of each model is contingent on the
accuracy of the forecasts for those independent variables. If the
weather forecast is off, then our cyclist volume forecast will also be
off. This is a limitation of any model that relies on exogenous inputs.

Now consider how close the forecasts were between XGBoost and OLS.

```{r}

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = date, y = Cyclists, group = Model)) +
  geom_line(aes(color = Model, linetype = Model, size = Model)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Actual" = "black", "OLS" = "blue", "XGBoost" = "darkgreen", "ARIMAX" = "red")) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("Actual" = "solid", "OLS" = "dotdash", "XGBoost" = "dashed", "ARIMAX" = "dashed")) +
  scale_size_manual(values = c("Actual" = 1.2, "OLS" = 0.8, "XGBoost" = 1, "ARIMAX" = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Forecast Evaluation: Actual vs Predicted Cyclist Counts",
    subtitle = "November 2025 Out-of-Sample Model Comparison",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Number of Cyclists"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "top"
  )
```

Both architectures track the same sudden dips and peaks across the
November production window because they share a fundamental reliance on
identical exogenous features. Unlike the ARIMAX framework, which derives
its momentum from its own historical lags, both OLS and XGBoost evaluate
each day based purely on the structural conditions provided to them,
such as calendar indicators and daily weather variations. When a sharp
weather event or a weekend shift occurs, both models immediately react
to the exact same external shocks.

This overlapping behavior strongly suggests that the primary
relationships driving daily cyclist volumes are predominantly linear and
additive in nature. While XGBoost is a highly flexible and is able to
capture non-linear interactions, it will approximate simpler,
linear-like step functions if the true underlying data-generating
process does not demand high-dimensional complexity.

The fact that XGBoost yields a superior set of evaluation metrics
despite looking visually twins with OLS indicates that it is not
discovering an entirely separate seasonal trend, but is instead handling
the extreme boundaries of the data more effectively. Where the rigid
assumptions of OLS cause it to overshoot or over-penalize on volatile
days, the tree-based structure of XGBoost keeps its predictions more
tightly bounded, capturing subtle thresholds in commuter behavior
without losing the shared structural signal.


## Conclusion

The development and deployment of this end-to-end time series pipeline provides a rigorous, data-driven framework for understanding and predicting daily cyclist volumes on the Johnson Street Bridge infrastructure. By evaluating and benchmarking classical econometric architectures against advanced machine learning methodologies, this investigation uncovers critical structural insights that balance forecasting accuracy with policy legibility.



The empirical results from the production window demonstrate that while each model successfully captured the overarching rhythm of urban active transportation, their operational mechanics yielded distinct performance profiles. The classical Ordinary Least Squares architecture provided a highly interpretable baseline, confirming fundamental economic and behavioral theories. The model clearly quantified how microclimatic volatility—specifically ambient temperature bounds, rainfall accumulation, and wind velocity—directly alters a cyclist's morning modal choice before commuting. Furthermore, the temporal variables within the OLS framework mathematically isolated a heavy midweek commuter pattern, indicating that the bridge serves primarily as a critical occupational artery rather than a purely recreational pathway.


However, the rigid global assumptions embedded within OLS severely limited its predictive boundaries, particularly regarding the deflation of standard errors caused by serial correlation. By extending this historical tracking into an ARIMAX framework, the pipeline successfully utilized an extensive lag architecture to absorb the internal momentum of the time series. Residual diagnostics for the ARIMAX model proved its statistical validity, showing a stable, mean-reverting error process centered near zero and a near-complete clearing of historical dependencies within the Autocorrelation and Partial Autocorrelation structures. The subtle, isolated boundary breaches remaining at bi-weekly intervals merely reflect real-world, non-linear human routines—such as employment pay cycles or statutory holiday shifts—that a linear structure cannot perfectly smooth out.


From an urban planning perspective, the implications of these models extend far beyond simple numerical accuracy. Because both the econometric and machine learning frameworks share a heavy reliance on identical exogenous features, their shared movements prove that daily cycling demand is highly sensitive to immediate environmental shocks. This sensitivity highlights a common pitfall in municipal planning: relying on static historical averages can leave cities unprepared for rapid shifts in transit behavior. By deploying this analysis, Municipalities can utilize these daily volume projections to optimize seasonal maintenance windows, manage trail congestion, allocate safety resources, and accurately evaluate the return on investment for expanded active transportation networks. Most importantly, understanding the underlying environmental and temporal mechanisms driving demand allows policymakers to better anticipate structural breaks, such as sudden shifts following the installation of protected bike lanes, ensuring that long-term urban planning remains resilient, proactive, and effective.
